the 3 alpha-azido-derivatives of cholic acid and taurocholic acid bind specifically to human high-density lipoprotiens, and that the binding is due to a photoaffinity labeling of three proteins of M(r) = 41,000 (alpha 1-acid-glycoprotein), M(r) =50,000 (alpha-1-antitripsin) and M(r) =83,000 (transferrin).

the affinity of bile acid conjugates to human high-density lipopropteins depends on the substituents at position 3, 7 and 12, the 3 beta-hydroxy-7 alpha, 12 alpha-dihydroy- and 3 beta-azi-7 alpha, -12 alpha-dihydropy-choleic acids showing a 23- and 20-fold higher affinity to HDL compared with 3 beta-hydroycholate,
the binding of bile acids is a complex process that involves multiple binding proteins, and that the affinity of the bile acid for the protein depends on the nature of the bile acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the proteins binding to conjugated and unconjuagted bile acids in human blood.
the elucidation of the mechanism of bile acid binding to serum proteins.
the identification of the serum proteins which are involved in the transport and metabolism of bile acids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

human serum contains at least five proteins which bind bile acids, the major one being albumin, followed by apolipoprotein A-I of high-density lipopropteins, alpha 1-acide glycoprotein, alpha 1-anti-trypsin and transferrin.

bile acid binding proteins are not only albumin and the lipoproteins, but also alpha 1-acider glycoprotein, alpha 1-anti trypsin, transferrin and probably also alpha 1-feto protein, alpha 1-HS glycoprotein, haptoglobin, hemopexine, alpha 2-macroglobulin, alpha 2-glycoprotein and ceruloplasmin.

the binding of bile acids and bile acid derivatives to human serum proteins depends upon several factors: the nature of the bile acid, its degree of hydrophobicity, the nature of the substituent in the 3-position of the steroid nucleus, and the nature of the binding protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of bile acids and bile salts is mediated by a variety of serum proteins, which are in part different from those involved in the transport of neutral lipids.
